q1: SELECT ITM.ITEMN, ITPV.VENDN FROM ITM ITM, (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN FROM ITP ITP, PUR PUR WHERE ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM AND PUR.ODATE > 85) ITPV WHERE ITM.ITEMN = ITPV.ITEMN AND ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITM.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN FROM ITM ITM, ITP ITP, PUR PUR WHERE ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM AND ITM.ITEMN = ITP.ITEMN AND PUR.ODATE > 85 AND ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 uses a subquery with DISTINCT on (ITEMN, VENDN) before joining with ITM, while Q2 applies DISTINCT after joining all three tables. This can lead to different results when there are multiple PUR records for the same ITEMN-VENDN combination.
counterexample: INSERT INTO ITM (ITEMN, TYPE) VALUES (10, 1); INSERT INTO ITP (ITEMN, PONUM) VALUES (10, 100), (10, 200); INSERT INTO PUR (PONUM, ODATE, VENDN) VALUES (100, 90, 50), (200, 90, 50);
counterexample_dsp: When an ITEMN has multiple PUR records with the same VENDN but different PONUMs, Q1 will deduplicate before joining with ITM, while Q2 will produce duplicate rows that get removed by DISTINCT only at the end. If ITM has ITEMN=10 that appears in multiple ITP-PUR joins with the same VENDN, Q1 returns one row while Q2 returns multiple identical rows that get collapsed to one by DISTINCT - making them appear equivalent. However, the real difference emerges when we consider ITEMN values that don't exist in ITM but appear in the subquery.

q1: SELECT Z.A, Z.B FROM R1 X, R2 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.A = Y.A AND Y.A = Z.A AND X.A = Z.A AND Y.B = Z.B
q2: SELECT Z.A, Z.B FROM R1 X, R2 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.A = Y.A AND Y.A = Z.A AND X.A = Z.A
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 has an additional condition Y.B = Z.B that Q2 lacks. Since R2 has a primary key on A, each A value can have only one row in R2, but different A values can have the same B values. The Y.B = Z.B condition in Q1 requires that the B values of Y and Z match, while Q2 only requires that their A values match through the join conditions.
counterexample_dsp: The difference occurs when there are multiple rows in R2 with the same B value but different A values. Q1 requires Y.B = Z.B, so if Y and Z have different B values (even with the same A value due to primary key constraint), Q1 returns no rows while Q2 returns rows.

q1: SELECT ITEMPRICE.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMNO AS ITN, ITP.NP AS NP FROM ITP ITP WHERE ITP.NP > 1000) ITEMPRICE, ITM ITM WHERE ITEMPRICE.ITN = ITM.ITEMNO
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM ITP ITP, ITM ITM WHERE ITP.NP > 1000 AND ITP.ITEMNO = ITM.ITEMNO
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 first applies DISTINCT to ITP records with NP > 1000 before joining with ITM, while Q2 joins first and then applies DISTINCT to the combined result. This can produce different results when there are multiple ITP records with the same ITEMNO and NP > 1000 that join to the same ITM record.
counterexample_dsp: When there are multiple ITP records with the same ITEMNO and NP > 1000 that join to the same ITM record, Q1 will deduplicate before joining (producing 1 row), while Q2 will join first and then deduplicate (producing multiple identical rows that get reduced to 1 row). However, the key difference is that Q1's DISTINCT is applied only to ITP columns before the join, while Q2's DISTINCT is applied to the full result set after the join.

q1: SELECT ITM.ITEMNO, ITEMPRICE.NP FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMNO AS ITN, ITP.NP AS NP FROM ITP ITP) ITEMPRICE, ITM ITM WHERE ITEMPRICE.ITN = ITM.ITEMNO
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITM.ITEMNO, ITP.NP FROM ITP ITP, ITM ITM WHERE ITP.ITEMNO = ITM.ITEMNO
explanation: Q1 first applies DISTINCT to ITP before joining with ITM, which removes duplicate ITEMNO-NP pairs from ITP. Q2 joins ITP and ITM first, then applies DISTINCT to the entire result set. This difference matters when ITP has multiple rows with the same ITEMNO but different NP values.
counterexample: INSERT INTO ITM (ITEMNO, TYPE) VALUES (1, 10); INSERT INTO ITP (ITEMNO, NP) VALUES (1, 100); INSERT INTO ITP (ITEMNO, NP) VALUES (1, 200);
counterexample_dsp: When ITP contains multiple rows with the same ITEMNO but different NP values, Q1 will remove these duplicates before joining, resulting in only one row per ITEMNO from ITP. Q2 will join first, potentially creating multiple rows for the same ITEMNO (with different NP values), and then DISTINCT will keep all unique combinations of ITEMNO and NP.

q1: SELECT * FROM ITP ITP WHERE ITP.ITEMN IN (SELECT ITL.ITEMN FROM ITL ITL WHERE ITL.WKCEN = 468 AND ITL.LOCAN = 0)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.* FROM ITP ITP, ITL ITL WHERE ITP.ITEMN = ITL.ITEMN AND ITL.WKCEN = 468 AND ITL.LOCAN = 0
explanation: Q1 uses a subquery to filter ITP rows where ITEMN exists in ITL with WKCEN=468 and LOCAN=0, potentially returning duplicate ITP rows if multiple matching ITL rows exist. Q2 performs an inner join and uses DISTINCT, eliminating duplicates. The key difference is that Q1 can return duplicate ITP rows while Q2 always returns distinct ITP rows.
counterexample: INSERT INTO ITP (ITEMN, PONUM) VALUES (1, 100); INSERT INTO ITL (ITEMN, WKCEN, LOCAN) VALUES (1, 468, 0); INSERT INTO ITL (ITEMN, WKCEN, LOCAN) VALUES (1, 468, 0);
counterexample_dsp: When there are multiple ITL rows with the same ITEMN, WKCEN=468, and LOCAN=0, Q1 will return duplicate ITP rows for that ITEMN, while Q2's DISTINCT will eliminate duplicates.

q1: SELECT T.TMEMBER FROM DEPTS D, TEAMS T WHERE D.DPROJ = T.TPROJ AND D.DNAME = 'SECURITY'
q2: SELECT V1.E FROM (SELECT D.DNAME AS D, D.DPROJ AS P, P.EMPL AS E FROM DEPTS D, PAYROLL P WHERE D.DNAME = P.PDEPT) V1, (SELECT T.TMEMBER AS E, P.PDEPT AS D, T.TPROJ AS P FROM TEAMS T, PAYROLL P WHERE T.TMEMBER = P.EMPL) V2 WHERE V1.D = 'SECURITY' AND V1.P = V2.P AND V1.E = V2.E AND V1.D = V2.D
explanation: Q1 finds team members working on projects managed by the 'SECURITY' department by joining DEPTS and TEAMS directly. Q2 uses two subqueries that join with PAYROLL and then joins them, requiring additional conditions that may filter out results present in Q1. The key difference is that Q2 requires team members to have payroll records matching the department, while Q1 does not reference PAYROLL at all.
counterexample: INSERT INTO DEPTS (DNAME, DPROJ) VALUES (1, 100); INSERT INTO TEAMS (TMEMBER, TPROJ) VALUES (999, 100);
counterexample_dsp: A team member works on a project managed by the 'SECURITY' department but has no corresponding record in PAYROLL (or has a different department in PAYROLL). Q1 returns this member, Q2 does not.

q1: SELECT Y.* FROM PAYROLL X, APPLICANT Y WHERE X.SSNO = Y.SSNO AND X.DEPTNO = 29
q2: SELECT C.* FROM PAYROLL A, (SELECT Y.SSNO, Y.DEPTNO FROM PAYROLL Y) B, APPLICANT C WHERE A.SSNO = B.SSNO AND C.SSNO = A.SSNO AND B.DEPTNO = 29
schema:
CREATE TABLE PAYROLL (SSNO INT, DEPTNO INT);
CREATE TABLE APPLICANT (SSNO INT, JOBTITILE INT, OFFICENO INT);
explanation: Q1 performs a simple join between PAYROLL and APPLICANT filtering on DEPTNO=29. Q2 creates a redundant self-join on PAYROLL and applies the DEPTNO filter to the wrong table (B instead of A), which can return different results when employees have multiple departments.
counterexample: INSERT INTO PAYROLL (SSNO, DEPTNO) VALUES (1, 29); INSERT INTO PAYROLL (SSNO, DEPTNO) VALUES (1, 30); INSERT INTO APPLICANT (SSNO, JOBTITILE, OFFICENO) VALUES (1, 100, 101);
counterexample_dsp: An employee (SSNO=1) works in department 29 (in PAYROLL table A) but also has another department record (DEPTNO=30 in PAYROLL table B). Q1 returns the APPLICANT record because A.DEPTNO=29, but Q2 returns nothing because B.DEPTNO=29 filter fails.

q1: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)
q2: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X, DEPT Y WHERE X.DEPT = Y.DEPT AND Y.LOC = 3 AND X.EMP = Y.MGR
schema:
CREATE TABLE EMP (NAME INT, DEPT INT, EMP INT);
CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPT INT, LOC INT, MGR INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 uses a subquery with tuple comparison (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT ...), which requires both EMP and DEPT values to match exactly with a row from the subquery. Q2 performs an inner join between EMP and DEPT on X.DEPT = Y.DEPT and then filters for X.EMP = Y.MGR and Y.LOC = 3. The key difference is that Q1's tuple comparison requires both fields to match the same subquery row, while Q2's join conditions could match different rows from DEPT for the same EMP record.
counterexample: INSERT INTO EMP (NAME, DEPT, EMP) VALUES (1, 10, 100); INSERT INTO DEPT (DEPT, LOC, MGR) VALUES (10, 3, 200), (20, 3, 100);
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample involves an EMP record that matches the DEPT condition with one row in DEPT (same DEPT and LOC=3) and the MGR condition with a different row in DEPT (same MGR but different DEPT). In this case, Q1 returns no results because no single DEPT row satisfies both conditions simultaneously, while Q2 returns the EMP record because the join conditions are satisfied across different DEPT rows.

q1: SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R X WHERE X.A = 5 AND X.C < 1
q2: SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R X WHERE X.A < 10
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT, C INT);
explanation: Q1 filters for rows where A = 5 AND C < 1, while Q2 filters for rows where A < 10. Q1 has stricter conditions (specific A value and C constraint) that are not equivalent to Q2's broader A range filter.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (A, B, C) VALUES (5, 10, 2);
counterexample_dsp: A row with A=5 and C=2 satisfies Q2's condition (A<10) but fails Q1's condition (C<1), showing Q1 is more restrictive.

q1:
SELECT 
    P.UID,
    P.UNAME,
    COALESCE(Q.CNT, 0) AS CNT
FROM (
    SELECT X.UID, X.UNAME
    FROM USER X
    WHERE X.CITY = 3
) AS P
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT Y.UID, COUNT(*) AS CNT
    FROM PICTURE Y
    WHERE Y.SIZE > 1000000
    GROUP BY Y.UID
) AS Q
USING (UID);
q2: SELECT X.UID AS UID, X.UNAME AS UNAME, COUNT(*) AS CNT FROM USER X, PICTURE Y WHERE X.UID = Y.UID AND Y.SIZE > 1000000 AND X.CITY = 3 GROUP BY X.UID, X.UNAME
schema:
CREATE TABLE USER (UID INT, UNAME INT, CITY INT);
CREATE TABLE PICTURE (UID INT, SIZE INT);
explanation: Q1 uses a LEFT JOIN and COALESCE to include all users from CITY=3, showing count=0 for users with no matching pictures. Q2 uses an INNER JOIN and COUNT(*) which excludes users with no matching pictures and shows actual counts only for users with matching pictures.
counterexample: INSERT INTO USER (UID, UNAME, CITY) VALUES (1, 101, 3); INSERT INTO USER (UID, UNAME, CITY) VALUES (2, 102, 3); INSERT INTO PICTURE (UID, SIZE) VALUES (2, 2000000);
counterexample_dsp: A user from CITY=3 with no pictures meeting SIZE>1000000 will appear in Q1 with CNT=0 but will be excluded from Q2 entirely.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.USRUID AS XID, X.USRNAME AS XNAME FROM USR X, PIC U, PIC V, PIC W WHERE X.USRUID = U.PICUID AND X.USRUID = V.PICUID AND X.USRUID = W.PICUID AND W.PICSIZE = V.PICSIZE AND U.PICSIZE < 500000 and V.PICSIZE >= 500000
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.USRUID AS XID, X.USRNAME AS XNAME FROM USR X, PIC U, PIC V WHERE X.USRUID = U.PICUID AND X.USRUID = V.PICUID AND U.PICSIZE < 500000 and V.PICSIZE >= 500000
schema:
CREATE TABLE USR (USRUID INT, USRNAME VARCHAR);
CREATE TABLE PIC (PICUID INT, PICSIZE INT);
explanation: Q1 requires the user to have at least three pictures (U, V, W) with specific size conditions including W.PICSIZE = V.PICSIZE, while Q2 only requires two pictures (U, V) with the size conditions. Q1 is more restrictive due to the additional W picture requirement and the equality condition.
counterexample: INSERT INTO USR (USRUID, USRNAME) VALUES (1, 'Alice'); INSERT INTO PIC (PICUID, PICSIZE) VALUES (1, 400000); INSERT INTO PIC (PICUID, PICSIZE) VALUES (1, 600000);
counterexample_dsp: A user has exactly two pictures: one small (<500000) and one large (>=500000). Q2 returns this user, but Q1 doesn't because it requires a third picture W that matches V's size.

q1: SELECT X.PNUM AS XP FROM PARTS X WHERE (X.PNUM, X.QOH) IN (SELECT Y.PNUM, COUNT(Y.SHIPDATE) AS CNT FROM SUPPLY Y WHERE Y.SHIPDATE < 10)
q2: SELECT X.PNUM AS XP FROM PARTS X, (SELECT Y.PNUM AS SUPPNUM, COUNT(Y.SHIPDATE) AS CT FROM SUPPLY Y WHERE Y.SHIPDATE < 10 GROUP BY Y.PNUM) TEMP WHERE X.QOH = TEMP.CT AND X.PNUM = TEMP.SUPPNUM
schema:
CREATE TABLE PARTS (PNUM INT, QOH INT);
CREATE TABLE SUPPLY (PNUM INT, SHIPDATE INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 uses an IN clause with a subquery that has no GROUP BY, making it syntactically invalid and logically different from Q2 which properly groups and aggregates. Q1's subquery would return multiple rows with the same PNUM but different counts, while Q2 groups by PNUM first.
counterexample: INSERT INTO PARTS VALUES (1, 2); INSERT INTO SUPPLY VALUES (1, 5); INSERT INTO SUPPLY VALUES (1, 3);
counterexample_dsp: A scenario where multiple SUPPLY records exist for the same PNUM with SHIPDATE < 10, causing Q1's subquery to return duplicate PNUM values with different counts, while Q2 properly aggregates by PNUM.

q1: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)
q2: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X
schema:
CREATE TABLE EMP (NAME INT, DEPT INT, EMP INT);
CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPT INT, LOC INT, MGR INT);
explanation: Q1 filters employees based on a condition involving department location and manager relationships, while Q2 returns all employees without any filtering. Q1 only returns employees who are managers of departments located at LOC=3, whereas Q2 returns all employees regardless of their role or department location.
counterexample: INSERT INTO EMP (NAME, DEPT, EMP) VALUES (1, 10, 100), (2, 20, 200); INSERT INTO DEPT (DEPT, LOC, MGR) VALUES (10, 3, 100), (20, 4, 200);
counterexample_dsp: When there are employees who are not managers of departments at LOC=3, Q1 will exclude them while Q2 includes them. Also, if there are no departments at LOC=3, Q1 returns empty results while Q2 returns all employees.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS AX FROM A X, B Y WHERE X.YA = Y.YB
q2:
SELECT X.X AS AX
FROM A X, A Y, B Z
WHERE X.X = Y.X
  AND X.YA = Z.YB

UNION ALL

SELECT 1 AS AX
FROM A X
WHERE 1 = 0;
schema:
CREATE TABLE A (X INT, YA INT);
CREATE TABLE B (YB INT);
explanation: Q1 finds distinct X values from table A where there exists at least one matching row in table B (X.YA = Y.YB). Q2 finds X values from table A where there exists another row in A with the same X value AND there exists a matching row in B, plus an empty UNION ALL that adds nothing. The key difference is that Q2 requires at least two rows in A with the same X value, while Q1 does not.
counterexample: INSERT INTO A (X, YA) VALUES (1, 10); INSERT INTO B (YB) VALUES (10);
counterexample_dsp: When there is only one row in table A that has a matching row in table B, Q1 will return that X value but Q2 will return nothing because it requires at least two rows in A with the same X value.

q1: SELECT X.X AS AX FROM A X WHERE X.YX = 'HELLO'
q2: SELECT X.X AS AX FROM A X WHERE X.YX = 'HELLO HI'
schema: CREATE TABLE A (X INT, YA INT, YX VARCHAR);
explanation: Q1 filters for rows where YX equals 'HELLO', while Q2 filters for rows where YX equals 'HELLO HI'. These are different string literals, so the queries filter on different conditions and are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample: INSERT INTO A (X, YA, YX) VALUES (1, 100, 'HELLO'); INSERT INTO A (X, YA, YX) VALUES (2, 200, 'HELLO HI');
counterexample_dsp: Insert a row where YX is 'HELLO' and another where YX is 'HELLO HI'. Q1 will return the row with 'HELLO', while Q2 will return the row with 'HELLO HI'.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS X FROM R1 X, R2 Y WHERE X.Y = Y.Y AND X.X = 1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS X FROM R1 X, R1 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.X = Y.X AND X.Y = Z.Y AND X.X = 1
schema:
CREATE TABLE R1 (X INT, Y INT);
CREATE TABLE R2 (Y INT);
explanation: Q1 finds distinct X values from R1 where X=1 and there exists at least one matching Y in R2. Q2 finds distinct X values from R1 where X=1 and there exists another row in R1 with the same X value and a Y that exists in R2. The key difference is that Q2 requires at least two rows in R1 with X=1 that share a common Y value existing in R2, while Q1 only requires one such row.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R1 (X, Y) VALUES (1, 10); INSERT INTO R2 (Y) VALUES (10);
counterexample_dsp: When R1 has only one row with X=1 that has a Y value present in R2, Q1 returns {1} but Q2 returns empty because it requires at least two rows in R1 with X=1.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A2 = X.A3
q2: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A1 = X.A3
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A1 INT, A2 INT, A3 INT);
explanation: Both queries are semantically equivalent because they select all rows from table R where all three columns A1, A2, and A3 have the same value. The conditions X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A2 = X.A3 (Q1) and X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A1 = X.A3 (Q2) both enforce that A1 = A2 = A3 through transitivity of equality.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.* FROM R X, R Y
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.* FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Both queries return all distinct rows from table R. Q1 performs a cross join of R with itself (R X, R Y) but only selects columns from X, making it equivalent to simply selecting from R with DISTINCT. The cross join doesn't affect the final result since we're only selecting from one side and applying DISTINCT.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT Y.A AS A FROM R X, R Y WHERE X.A = Y.A
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.A AS A FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT);
explanation: Both queries return the same set of distinct A values from table R. Q1 performs a self-join on R where X.A = Y.A, but since it's an equality condition on the same attribute and only selects Y.A with DISTINCT, it effectively returns all distinct A values from R, which is identical to Q2's SELECT DISTINCT X.A FROM R X.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT Y.A1 AS A1, Y.A2 AS A2 FROM R X, R Y WHERE X.A1 = Y.A1 AND X.A2 = Y.A2
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.A1 AS A1, X.A2 AS A2 FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A1 INT, A2 INT);
explanation: Both queries return the same set of distinct (A1, A2) pairs from table R. Q1 performs a self-join on equality of both columns but this doesn't filter or transform the data - it just creates duplicates that DISTINCT removes, making it equivalent to Q2 which directly selects distinct pairs from R.

q1: SELECT X.A, SUM(X.A + X.B) FROM R X GROUP BY X.A
q2: SELECT Y.A, SUM(Y.A + Y.B) FROM R Y GROUP BY Y.A
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Both queries are semantically equivalent. Q1 and Q2 perform identical operations: grouping by column A and computing the sum of (A + B) for each group. The only difference is the table alias (X vs Y), which does not affect the query logic or results.

q1: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50) Y WHERE Y.X < 200
q2: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X < 200) Y WHERE Y.X > 50
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Both queries filter table R for rows where X is between 50 and 200. Q1 first filters for X > 50 then for X < 200, while Q2 first filters for X < 200 then for X > 50. The order of applying these range filters does not affect the final result, as both require both conditions to be true simultaneously.

q1: SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50 AND X.X < 200
q2: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50) Y WHERE Y.X < 200
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Both queries filter rows from table R where column X is between 50 and 200 (exclusive). Q1 does this with a single WHERE clause, while Q2 uses a subquery to first filter X > 50 and then filter X < 200 on the result. The logic is identical and produces the same result set.

q1: SELECT COUNT(*) AS A FROM R X
q2: SELECT COUNT(Y.B) FROM R Y
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Q1 counts all rows in table R regardless of NULL values, while Q2 counts only non-NULL values in column B. They are not equivalent when column B contains NULL values.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (A, B) VALUES (1, 10); INSERT INTO R (A, B) VALUES (2, NULL); INSERT INTO R (A, B) VALUES (3, 30);
counterexample_dsp: When table R contains rows where column B has NULL values, Q1 will count all rows but Q2 will exclude rows with NULL in B from the count.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50 OR X.X < 200
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Q1 selects all rows where X > 50 OR X < 200, which includes all rows except those where X is exactly 50 or exactly 200 (and NULL values). Q2 uses UNION ALL to combine rows where X > 50 and rows where X < 200, which duplicates rows where X satisfies both conditions (i.e., 51-199).
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (X) VALUES (100);
counterexample_dsp: Insert a row with X = 100, which satisfies both X > 50 and X < 200. Q1 returns it once due to DISTINCT, but Q2 returns it twice due to UNION ALL.

q1: SELECT DEPT.NAME AS DNAME, COUNT(*) AS C FROM DEPT AS DEPT GROUP BY DEPT.NAME HAVING DEPT.NAME = 10
q2: SELECT T2.DNAME, T2.CNT AS C FROM (SELECT DEPT0.NAME AS DNAME, COUNT(*) AS CNT FROM DEPT AS DEPT0 GROUP BY DEPT0.NAME) AS T2 WHERE T2.DNAME = 10
schema: CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPTNO INT, NAME INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 applies the WHERE condition (DEPT.NAME = 10) before grouping, while Q2 applies it after grouping. This can lead to different results when there are multiple departments with the same NAME value.
counterexample: INSERT INTO DEPT (DEPTNO, NAME) VALUES (1, 10); INSERT INTO DEPT (DEPTNO, NAME) VALUES (2, 10); INSERT INTO DEPT (DEPTNO, NAME) VALUES (3, 20);
counterexample_dsp: When there are multiple departments with NAME = 10, Q1 groups them together and counts all rows, while Q2 filters after grouping and shows each group separately. Also, when there are departments with NAME ≠ 10, Q1 excludes them before grouping, while Q2 includes them in the grouping phase and then filters them out.

q1: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 0) Y WHERE Y.X > 0
q2: SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 0
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Both queries filter table R for rows where X > 0. Q1 uses a redundant subquery that applies the same filter twice, but this doesn't change the result since the condition X.X > 0 is identical in both the inner and outer queries.

q1: SELECT * FROM A X WHERE X.C IN (SELECT Y.C FROM A Y)
q2: SELECT * FROM A X
schema: CREATE TABLE A (C INT);
explanation: Both queries return all rows from table A. Q1's subquery (SELECT Y.C FROM A Y) returns all C values from table A, so the condition X.C IN (all C values from A) is always true for every row X in A, making Q1 equivalent to Q2.

q1: SELECT X.A1 AS A1, X.A2 AS A2, Y.B1 AS B1, Y.B2 AS B2 FROM A X, B Y WHERE X.A1 = Y.B1
q2: SELECT Y.A1 AS A1, Y.A2 AS A2, X.B1 AS B1, X.B2 AS B2 FROM B X, A Y WHERE Y.A1 = X.B1
schema:
CREATE TABLE A (A1 INT, A2 INT);
CREATE TABLE B (B1 INT, B2 INT);
explanation: Both queries perform an inner join between tables A and B on A.A1 = B.B1, and both return the same four columns (A1, A2, B1, B2) with identical values. The only difference is table aliasing - Q1 uses X for A and Y for B, while Q2 uses Y for A and X for B, but this doesn't affect the result since column aliases explicitly map to the correct source columns.

q1: SELECT * FROM R1 X, (SELECT * FROM R2 UNION ALL SELECT * FROM R3) Y
explanation: Q1 performs a cross join between R1 and the union of R2 and R3, while Q2 performs a union of cross joins between R1 and R2, and R1 and R3. The key difference is that Q1 produces one result set with all combinations, while Q2 produces two separate result sets concatenated together. When R1 has multiple rows, Q1 will generate all combinations of R1 rows with each row from the union, while Q2 will duplicate R1 rows in the output structure.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R1 VALUES (1); INSERT INTO R1 VALUES (2); INSERT INTO R2 VALUES (10); INSERT INTO R3 VALUES (20);
counterexample_dsp: When R1 has 2 rows, R2 has 1 row, and R3 has 1 row, Q1 produces 4 rows (2 × 2) while Q2 produces 4 rows but with different row ordering and structure - specifically, Q2 groups all R1×R2 combinations first, then all R1×R3 combinations.

q1: SELECT X.B AS XB, Y.B AS YB FROM R1 X, R2 Y
q2: SELECT X1.XB AS XB, Y1.YB AS YB FROM (SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R1 X) X1, (SELECT Y.B AS YB FROM R2 Y) Y1
schema:
CREATE TABLE R1 (A INT, B INT);
CREATE TABLE R2 (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Both queries perform a cross join between all rows from R1 and R2, selecting only the B column from each table. Q1 does this directly with a Cartesian product, while Q2 first creates subqueries that select only the B columns from each table, then performs the cross join on these subqueries. The final result set is identical in both cases - all combinations of B values from R1 and R2.

q1: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R UNION ALL SELECT * FROM S) X
